scope: First13 finite named/example written reaction models supporting1.25; not the full prescribed collection or a processed-paper/template bank.

models.title: Balance magnesium combustion and its solid product
models.condition: Magnesium burns in oxygen in the stated oxide-formation model; the oxide is a solid. This is a supervised experimental context, not an experiment performed here.
models.interpretationLimit: Air combustion can have other contributions, including nitride formation; the named oxide model does not prove a collected sample is pure MgO. Source1.36 permits combustion or reduction, not compulsory performance of both.

practice.question: The supplied product is magnesium oxide MgO. Correct Mg(s) + O₂(g) → MgO₂(s) without changing the supplied product identity, then check all atoms.
practice.answer: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s). Magnesium oxide is MgO, not MgO₂. Two MgO units contain two O atoms, so use one O₂ and two Mg; each side has Mg₂O₂.

models.title: Retain oxygen when copper(II) oxide is reduced
models.condition: This supplied reduction model uses hydrogen over heated copper(II) oxide. Water is vapour in the hot reaction region and can condense to liquid on cooling.
models.interpretationLimit: It is a written supervised model, not a direction to improvise heating hydrogen. Copper oxide loses oxygen; hydrogen gains oxygen. The source gives CuO as a reduction example, not the only possible experimental route.

practice.question: Correct CuO(s) + H₂(g) → Cu(s) + H₂(g) using the supplied observation of water. Why might the hot-region equation use (g), while collected cool water is (l)?
practice.answer: CuO(s) + H₂(g) → Cu(s) + H₂O(g). Oxygen from CuO must appear in water, not vanish. At the stated hot region water is vapour; after cooling it can be H₂O(l). The phase label follows the stated conditions.

models.title: Model the products of molten lead(II) bromide — Paper 2C
models.condition: Electrolysis of molten PbBr₂: lead forms at the negative electrode and bromine at the positive electrode. This equation describes the hot molten apparatus, where the lead product is liquid; it becomes solid after cooling. Suitable inert electrodes are used in this model.
models.interpretationLimit: Use the phase appropriate to the location and temperature stated. Solid PbBr₂ does not have the same mobile-ion conduction as its melt. Electrolysis uses electrical energy; no water-derived ions belong in this molten case.

practice.question: Correct the product formula in PbBr₂(l) → Pb(l) + 2Br(g). State each electrode product and explain why the hot lead and cooled lead may have different state labels.
practice.answer: PbBr₂(l) → Pb(l) + Br₂(g). Bromine is diatomic Br₂, not two isolated Br atoms. Lead forms at the negative electrode and bromine at the positive; hot lead is liquid in this stated model and solidifies on cooling.

models.title: Include water in an aqueous chloride model — Paper 2C
models.condition: This chosen overall model uses sufficiently concentrated aqueous NaCl, suitable inert electrodes and separated products: H₂ at the negative electrode, Cl₂ at the positive, with NaOH left in solution.
models.interpretationLimit: Aqueous water participates. Chloride concentration and electrode conditions matter: oxygen can be favoured in dilute chloride conditions. The equation is not a guarantee for every aqueous NaCl setup or an undivided mixture in which products can react further.

practice.question: For the specified concentrated, inert-electrode, separated-product model, replace NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) → NaOH(aq) + HCl(g) with a balanced equation and name the two electrode gases.
practice.answer: 2NaCl(aq) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g) + Cl₂(g). Hydrogen forms at the negative electrode and chlorine at the positive. The model does not produce HCl as the electrode gas or discharge sodium metal from the aqueous solution.

models.wordEquation: sodium chloride + water → sodium hydroxide + hydrogen + chlorine

models.title: Keep sulfate in the aqueous copper model — Paper 2C
models.condition: Chosen overall model for aqueous CuSO₄ with suitable inert electrodes: copper is deposited at the negative electrode and oxygen forms at the positive electrode; the solution becomes more acidic.
models.interpretationLimit: Water supplies the oxygen and the sulfate remains in solution. This differs from using an active copper anode, which can dissolve instead of giving this oxygen model; do not transfer inert-electrode products blindly.

practice.question: A student writes CuSO₄(aq) → Cu(s) + S(s) + 2O₂(g). Correct this for the specified inert-electrode aqueous model and explain why sulfate does not have to become sulfur.
practice.answer: 2CuSO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l) → 2Cu(s) + O₂(g) + 2H₂SO₄(aq). Cu²⁺ gives deposited copper; water-derived species give oxygen at the anode. Sulfate remains in the acid-containing solution rather than becoming sulfur in this model.

models.wordEquation: copper(II) sulfate + water → copper + oxygen + sulfuric acid

models.title: Distinguish electrolyte from net water decomposition — Paper 2C
models.condition: Electrolyse water containing dilute sulfuric acid using suitable inert electrodes. Hydrogen forms at the negative electrode and oxygen at the positive; acid supplies ions for conduction but is not consumed in this overall model.
models.interpretationLimit: The ideal gas amount ratio is H₂:O₂ = 2:1 under matched collection conditions. Escaping gas, dissolution and collection differences can affect measured volumes. Do not describe sulfate decomposition as the required net change.

practice.question: A proposed overall equation consumes H₂SO₄ and produces SO₂. Replace it with the net water equation for the stated dilute-acid inert-electrode model and give the ideal gas ratio.
practice.answer: 2H₂O(l) → 2H₂(g) + O₂(g). Dilute sulfuric acid is the electrolyte in the stated overall model, not a consumed sulfur-containing reactant. Ideal H₂:O₂ amount ratio is 2:1; equal-temperature/pressure gas volumes have that same model ratio.

models.title: Use calcium’s charge before balancing the marble reaction
models.condition: Marble chips are modelled as solid CaCO₃ reacting with dilute aqueous HCl. The gas is CO₂; gas collection requires a suitable free outlet and comparable timing/conditions in a supervised plan.
models.interpretationLimit: The salt identity is fixed before adjusting coefficients: Ca²⁺ needs two chloride ions. Bubble production alone does not identify CO₂. The acid-excess condition must be stated if equal carbonate amounts are used to predict equal final gas amounts.

practice.question: Given Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻, correct CaCO₃ + HCl → CaCl + H₂O + CO₂, include states for the stated dilute-acid model, and name the gas test.
practice.answer: CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). CaCl₂ follows ion charges; then two HCl supply its chlorides and the two H for water. CO₂ clouds limewater in the appropriate separate supervised test.

models.wordEquation: calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide

models.title: Keep the water product in peroxide decomposition
models.condition: The required investigation compares different solids in the catalytic decomposition of approved dilute hydrogen peroxide solution. A suitable catalyst is shown as a condition, not consumed in the overall equation.
models.interpretationLimit: Faster gas production alone does not establish unchanged catalyst identity or equal active sites across different solids. No hydrogen gas is a product of this decomposition model.

practice.question: Correct H₂O₂(aq) → H₂(g) + O₂(g) using the supplied products water and oxygen. Give the balanced equation and oxygen test; should a catalyst appear as a consumed reactant?
practice.answer: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). Both sides have H₄O₄. Oxygen relights a glowing splint in the separate supervised test. A suitable catalyst belongs above the arrow/as a condition, not as a consumed overall reactant.

models.title: Account for all five waters during dehydration
models.condition: Controlled heating of blue CuSO₄·5H₂O removes water of crystallisation to give white anhydrous CuSO₄. This model represents the hot region, with water leaving as vapour.
models.interpretationLimit: More severe heating can cause other changes. An open tube can lose water and does not by itself establish a sealed dynamic equilibrium. The dot-water multiplier is not a new chemical element or a coefficient on CuSO₄.

practice.question: Complete CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) → CuSO₄(s) + H₂O(g). Explain the coefficient and why this colour change is not simply melting blue crystals into a white liquid.
practice.answer: CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) → CuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O(g). The left contains five water units, so five must leave. Dehydration changes the hydrated solid into anhydrous solid; blue-to-white is not a white liquid produced by simple melting.

models.wordEquation: hydrated copper(II) sulfate → anhydrous copper(II) sulfate + water

models.title: Model the reverse hydration with stated water conditions
models.condition: This chosen stoichiometric hydration model adds water to cooled anhydrous CuSO₄ to form blue pentahydrate and release energy. It uses liquid water, unlike vapour leaving the hot dehydration model.
models.interpretationLimit: A large excess of water can instead give a blue solution; the model does not guarantee isolated pure dry crystals from any addition. State labels reflect each described situation, not an unqualified reversal of the hot apparatus.

practice.question: Balance CuSO₄(s) + H₂O(l) → CuSO₄·5H₂O(s). Why does a blue appearance after a large water excess not establish pure dry hydrated crystals?
practice.answer: CuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O(l) → CuSO₄·5H₂O(s). Five water units are incorporated in the stated pentahydrate model. A large excess can dissolve the salt into a blue solution, so colour alone does not establish an isolated pure dry crystalline product.

models.wordEquation: anhydrous copper(II) sulfate + water → hydrated copper(II) sulfate

models.title: Name both gases before balancing the reversible example
models.condition: Controlled heating can form ammonia and hydrogen chloride gases; those gases can recombine in a cooler region to form white solid NH₄Cl. The reversible arrow describes these possible directions.
models.interpretationLimit: The white deposit is solid ammonium chloride, not white ammonia gas. An open demonstration is not a constant-temperature sealed-equilibrium measurement. It is a teacher-controlled model with irritating gases, not a sealed-heating procedure.

practice.question: Use the supplied products ammonia and hydrogen chloride to replace NH₄Cl(s) → N₂(g) + H₂(g) + Cl₂(g). Include states, balance and explain the white cooler-region deposit.
practice.answer: NH₄Cl(s) ⇌ NH₃(g) + HCl(g). Each side has N₁H₄Cl₁. The named gases can recombine to form solid NH₄Cl in a cooler region; chlorine gas and white ammonia are not the named products.

models.title: Distinguish neutralisation from hydrogen formation
models.condition: Chosen simple calorimetry example: aqueous hydrochloric acid neutralises aqueous sodium hydroxide, giving aqueous sodium chloride and liquid water under the stated dilute conditions.
models.interpretationLimit: Use total solution mass for a heat estimate but the reacting limiting amount for a molar result. A warming mixture alone needs controlled initial temperatures to support a reaction-heat inference.

practice.question: Correct HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂(g), using the supplied acid/alkali products. Is this the same gas-forming pattern as a suitable metal plus acid?
practice.answer: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l). Both sides have H₂ClNaO. Neutralisation forms water, whereas a suitable metal-plus-acid reaction can form hydrogen. Similar acid names do not make the product pattern identical.

models.wordEquation: hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium chloride + water

models.title: Keep the sulfate group intact in a displacement model
models.condition: Chosen displacement/calorimetry example: zinc reacts with aqueous CuSO₄ to give aqueous ZnSO₄ and solid copper. Under the relevant conditions zinc is more reactive than copper.
models.interpretationLimit: Sulfate stays as the sulfate group in this overall model; zinc is oxidised and Cu²⁺ reduced. An excess solid’s initial amount is not automatically the amount that reacts in calorimetry calculations.

practice.question: Given zinc sulfate and copper as the supplied products, write word and balanced formula equations with states for zinc plus aqueous copper(II) sulfate. Should sulfur appear as a product?
practice.answer: Zinc + copper(II) sulfate → zinc sulfate + copper. Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s). Both sides contain ZnCuSO₄; sulfate remains in solution with zinc rather than forming elemental sulfur.

models.wordEquation: zinc + copper(II) sulfate → zinc sulfate + copper
